sections.content_markdown: c. If the valencies of the two elements are divisible by a common number, then the quotient after dividing will be written following the formula stated in rule b. For example, carbon dioxide is a compound made of carbon and oxygen. Valencies of carbon and oxygen are $4$ and $2$ respectively. Since they can be divided by $2$, therefore, we have to write the quotients $	ext{C}_1	ext{O}_2$. Again, since $1$ is not necessary to mention, we will write, $	ext{CO}_2$. In the compound ferrous sulfate, the valency of ferrous is $2$ and that of sulfate ion ($	ext{SO}_4^{2-}$) is $2$. Therefore, after dividing them both with $2$, the formula stands $	ext{FeSO}_4$. Same way, valency of boron and nitrogen is $3$. Therefore, the formula of boron nitride stands $	ext{B}_3	ext{N}_3 = 	ext{B}_1	ext{N}_1 = 	ext{BN}$.

The formula of using symbols and the number of atoms of the kind/kinds of element(s) that constitute the molecule of an element or compound is called the molecular formula or chemical formula. We have just learned about it. Again, the formula of expressing a molecule through the symbols and bonds of atoms, otherwise known as organization of atoms, is called the structural formula. For example, three carbon atoms combine with eight hydrogen atoms and produce propane ($	ext{C}_3	ext{H}_8$) molecule. This $	ext{C}_3	ext{H}_8$ is the molecular or chemical formula of propane. Again, the three carbon atoms here bond with each other like a chain and the rest valencies get completed with hydrogen. Thus, valency of each carbon becomes $4$. The structural formula of propane is shown below:

$$\begin{array}{ccc}
\text{H} & \text{H} & \text{H} \\
| & | & | \\
\text{H}-\text{C} & -\text{C} & -\text{C}-\text{H} \\
| & | & | \\
\text{H} & \text{H} & \text{H}
\end{array}$$

Again, the molecular formula of water $	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$ is written in structural formula:

$$\begin{array}{c}
\text{O} \\
/ \backslash \\
\text{H} \quad \text{H}
\end{array}$$
